newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Weary crew mistake plunges Mir into new crisis.
newsitem.headline: Weary crew mistake plunges Mir into new crisis.

text.p: A weary cosmonaut aboard Russia's Mir space station mistakenly pulled out a vital computer cable on Thursday, plunging their crippled ship into its worst crisis since a near-fatal collision three weeks ago.

The three-man crew, whose commander developed a probably stress-induced heart problem this week, had to sit in their Soyuz escape capsule to communicate with Earth and were using flashlights to get around the darkened station.

"I should stress it is an especially unpleasant situation. It very much recalls the situation we were in after the crash," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control in Korolyov outside Moscow.

But the cosmonauts were in no immediate danger and had no plans to abandon ship even though lights, heating, communications and all non-vital systems were shut down on the main station, forcing them to rely on self-contained systems in the tiny Soyuz vessel moored alongside.
They even had orders to continue preparing for next week's risky repair job to fix cables damaged in the earlier accident -- although one NASA official said a delay seemed likely now.

Yet tension was palpable at Mission Control in the biggest drama since the June 25 collision -- also possibly caused by a crew error -- which cut power by up to half and nearly cost the crew their lives when one of Mir's modules was holed.
"Shut it down! Shut it down!" the duty mission controller barked into a microphone at Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev as the crew fought to save power.
"This was purely human error," Solovyov said of the latest crisis. Officials have neither confirmed nor denied reports that a basic mistake by Tsibliyev caused the original collision.

He would not say who of the two Russians and one American aboard pulled the computer plug. The crewman immediately replaced the cable, which was connected to the station's "logic block" computer system. But the damage was done.

The gyroscopic guidance system that keeps Mir's solar panels lined up to the Sun again malfunctioned -- it has been dogged by problems in the last three weeks -- driving the power supply down to the very minimum needed to keep the station running.

Solovyov said the crew were to press on with preparations for repairing the original damage. Tsibliyev, 43, was pulled from the two-man repair team on Wednesday after developing an irregular heartbeat. British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, is due to step in alongside engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39.

But they have just an hour of daylight during every two-hour orbit of the Earth and have other technical problems to contend with as well as possible signs of deep fatigue showing up in mistakes. So the repair schedule seemed in doubt.
"This will probably put a delay on the plans that we had," said Leroy Chiao, a NASA Shuttle astronaut working at Korolyov.
Russian officials have said that the job could be left for a Russian-French crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7.

The collision was the worst accident in Mir's 11 years in space but by no means an isolated mishap, raising questions abroad over whether it should be ditched before a new international space station goes into action from next year.
Russian officials, whose agency partly depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep the post-Soviet space industry afloat, insist they will not abandon the station.

But if conditions became untenable, the Mir crew could take to their Soyuz escape capsule and return home, probably condemning Mir to a premature end and posing a headache on Earth where the 140-tonne complex would come down with a crash.
